newsitem.title: USA: OLYMPICS-RESIGNED SALT LAKE WINTER GAMES CHIEF TO GET $1 MILLION.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-RESIGNED SALT LAKE WINTER GAMES CHIEF TO GET $1 MILLION.

text.p: Winter Olympics organisers voted Wednesday to give $1 million to the man who worked for more than a decade to bring the 2002 Games to Utah following his resignation in a wife-beating scandal.

Trustees of the Salt Lake Organising Committee (SLOC) also approved a resolution to retain Tom Welch as a consultant at $10,000 a month until the Games take place and to provide him with a pension of up to $500,000.
The unanimous votes came during a closed-door meeting of the trustees' executive committee, said SLOC spokesman Mike Korologos.
The meeting was prompted by Welch's resignation as SLOC president and chief executive officer eight days after he was charged with spousal battery. Welch has denied the charge.

The trustees also launched a search for a successor to Welch, although they named executive committee chairman Frank Joklik interim president and CEO and it was possible he would remain in the post through the 2002 Games, Korologos said.

One name high on the list of potential replacements for Welch was Dave Checketts, former president of the NBA's Utah Jazz and currently president of Madison Square Garden, which houses basketball's New York Knicks and hockey's New York Rangers.
Welch, a former Mormon bishop known in Utah as "Mr Olympics", attended Wednesday's meeting, but had no immediate comment.
Korologos said Welch would be given a future one-time lump sum payment of $1 million in recognition of his efforts to bring the Winter Games to Salt Lake City.

According to police, Welch was charged with domestic violence battery, based on allegations that he bruised and restrained his wife Alma during an argument over another woman. His wife did not press charges but authorities decided to go ahead with the case.
Welch, who was on an African safari with one of his six children when the charge was filed, denied hitting his wife, but acknowledged "emotional ties" to an unnamed woman.
When he resigned his post as SLOC chief, he said he was doing so to end the "feeding frenzy" surrounding the case in this staunchly conservative city that is home base for the Mormon Church.
"There are a lot of innocent people out here, including myself, who are getting devoured," Welch told reporters.

The Deseret News, which is owned by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints and reflects Mormon attitudes, said in an editorial the need to maintain the ultra-clean image was paramount in the deluge of news stories about Welch.
"Lest they tarnish the image Utah has tried to portray leading up to the Games, Welch needed to free SLOC from the burden he had become," it said.

Welch had worked since 1985 to bring the Winter Olympics to Utah. Salt Lake City lost out to Nagano, Japan, in the bid for the 1998 Olympics before landing the 2002 Games. He was named president and chief executive of the organising committee in 1995.

In Wednesday's editorial, the Deseret News said Welch's resignation was "for the best. The 2002 Winter Olympics are bigger than Tom Welch. They will put the entire state and its people on worldwide display."
The newspaper went on: "Welch was wise enough to understand how, even should he vindicate himself from the charges, his personal life had become too distracting."

However, it praised his work on behalf of Salt Lake City, saying: "Without his tireless efforts, both in the unsuccessful bid for the 1998 Games and the triumphant campaign for 2002, Utah would not be anxiously preparing to greet the world in five years."
